question:
Patient note:
A 93-year-old man, formerly a long-haul railway signal technician who now resides in a ground-floor apartment within an assisted-living complex, was brought to clinic late this afternoon by his niece for a general medical review requested by urology before scheduling transurethral resection of a bothersome bladder outlet obstruction. The niece reports that over the past four winters her uncle has gradually relinquished responsibility for household bookkeeping after repeatedly misplacing bank statements and forgetting the password to his retirement-fund website; he still recognizes relatives by name and remains gregarious, yet yesterday he could not recall what he had eaten for breakfast when reminded two hours later and he sometimes re-checks the front-door lock three or four times within a minute. On a three-item recall performed in the waiting room he produced only one word after five minutes despite intact repetition, and his clock drawing placed the hands at random angles, though he followed single-step directions and interpreted a simple proverb accurately. Ambulation is independent within the facility but limited to short corridors: he halts after roughly 50 meters because of a cramping, burning sensation in both calves that resolves within two minutes of standing still; he no longer attends morning walks to the nearby pond because an incline provokes the same discomfort. A duplex study ordered six months ago demonstrated diffuse femoropopliteal plaque with ankle–brachial indices of 0.54 on the right and 0.58 on the left, and a vascular-surgery consultation at that time recommended continued walking exercise and antiplatelet therapy without immediate intervention. He denies chest tightness, diaphoresis on exertion, or prior emergency visits for suspected coronary occlusion; electrocardiograms obtained during pre-operative evaluations for cataract surgery two and four years ago showed normal sinus rhythm without Q waves or segment shifts, serial high-sensitivity troponin values during an episode of viral gastroenteritis last year remained below the detection threshold, and he has never been hospitalized for a heart attack. He sleeps comfortably on a single pillow, climbs one flight of stairs with pauses only for leg pain rather than breathlessness, and has never been told that his heart’s pumping function is reduced; a transthoracic echocardiogram performed eighteen months ago for a soft systolic murmur revealed an ejection fraction of 62 % with normal chamber dimensions and trivial aortic sclerosis. He has never experienced slurred speech, facial droop, monocular vision loss, unilateral numbness, or brief spells of neurologic deficit suggestive of transient cerebral ischemia, and informal strength testing in the clinic room today demonstrated 5/5 power throughout with symmetric reflexes and flexor plantar responses. Pulmonary history is unremarkable: he never smoked, maintains oxygen saturation of 97 % on room air at rest, and last month’s chest radiograph taken for cough after an upper-respiratory infection showed clear lung fields without hyperinflation. Metabolic panels over the past decade have revealed fasting plasma glucose values ranging 92–106 mg/dL and a glycated hemoglobin of 5.9 % obtained last week; he adheres to a modest-carbohydrate breakfast of oatmeal and fruit and has never required medication for glycemic control. Long-standing hypertension is managed with amlodipine 5 mg each morning and low-dose aspirin 81 mg daily initiated by his primary physician after the ankle–brachial study; home readings provided by the niece average 128/64 mm Hg. The major laboratory concern is renal: serum creatinine has climbed steadily from 1.6 mg/dL five years ago to 2.8 mg/dL today, corresponding to an estimated glomerular filtration rate of 24 mL/min/1.73 m²; blood urea nitrogen is 48 mg/dL, potassium 4.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, and urinalysis shows 2+ protein with bland sediment. He has not developed uremic pruritus, pericarditic pain, or volume overload, but nephrology has discussed fistula planning should dialysis eventually become necessary. Hepatic indices remain within reference limits: alanine aminotransferase 25 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 27 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 82 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, albumin 4.0 g/dL, and international normalized ratio 1.0; abdominal ultrasound two years ago depicted a 13-cm smooth, homogeneous liver without steatosis, nodularity, portal-flow abnormality, or splenic enlargement, and the patient denies jaundice, pruritus, abdominal distention, or gastrointestinal bleeding. He has never suffered ulcer-like dyspepsia, upper-tract hemorrhage, or Helicobacter treatment. He reports no history of enlarged lymph nodes or blood cancers, and physical examination today reveals no lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly. HIV antibody testing performed two years ago as part of routine preoperative screening was nonreactive, and he has had no subsequent risk exposures. Current medications, all taken prior to today’s visit, include amlodipine as noted, aspirin 81 mg daily, cholecalciferol 1000 IU each morning, and an over-the-counter psyllium supplement for constipation; he developed a rash to sulfonamide antibiotics in his forties and avoids that class. He drinks half a glass of porter with Sunday lunch, stopped pipe tobacco after his retirement at age 65, and denies illicit drug use. Vital signs at 15:30 record temperature 36.6 °C, blood pressure 132/66 mm Hg seated right arm, heart rate 70 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 97 % on ambient air, weight 71 kg, height 175 cm, yielding a body-mass index of 23 kg/m². He appears well nourished but somewhat inattentive, occasionally repeating questions already answered. Examination shows a soft systolic ejection murmur grade 2/6 at the right upper sternal border, no gallops, and brisk carotid upstrokes without bruit. Lungs are clear with vesicular breath sounds throughout and no wheezes or crackles. The abdomen is flat, nontender, with a liver edge not palpable, no fluid wave, and active bowel sounds. Lower extremities reveal shiny, hairless shins, 1+ pitting edema to the ankles, and dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are appreciable only with Doppler; dependent rubor develops after thirty seconds of leg elevation and venous filling is delayed on dependency. Skin displays scattered actinic lentigines but no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory panel obtained today also notes hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, white-blood-cell count 5.6 × 10⁹/L, platelet count 235 × 10⁹/L, and a spot urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 680 mg/g. A 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm at 68 beats/min, PR interval 150 ms, QRS 88 ms, axis 15°, and no repolarization abnormalities. The urology team seeks guidance on peri-operative risk given limited renal reserve, strategies to mitigate post-operative delirium in light of his baseline cognitive deficits, and recommendations regarding continuation of antiplatelet therapy around the time of surgery.

Question: What is the patient's Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The age-adjusted Charlson Comorbidity Index sums age points and weighted comorbidities present before treatment.
- Age: 1 point at 50–59, 2 at 60–69, 3 at 70–79, and 4 at ≥80. At 93, he scores 4.
- Peripheral vascular disease: 1. Reproducible calf claudication, femoropopliteal plaque, and ankle–brachial indices of 0.54 and 0.58 establish symptomatic arterial disease.
- Dementia: 1. Progressive memory and executive impairment interferes with independent bookkeeping, supporting this category.
- Moderate-to-severe kidney disease: 2. His eGFR of 24 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates stage 4 CKD.
- Other CCI conditions: 0. No qualifying myocardial infarction, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, hemiplegia, chronic pulmonary disease, rheumatic disease, ulcer, liver disease, diabetes, malignancy, or AIDS is documented. Hypertension and bladder outlet obstruction do not score.
Total: 4 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 8.
Final answer: 8
